newsitem.title: USA: Cyprus promises concessions at New York talks.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus promises concessions at New York talks.

text.p: Cyprus' foreign minister pledged on Friday that his government would approach key talks over the divided island next month in a "spirit of give and take," ready to make concessions if the Turkish Cypriots did.

"We will go to the face-to-face negotiations with an open mind, having the political will to be constructive and positive and ready to negotiate a comprehensive solution to the Cyprus problem in a spirit of give and take," Ioannis Cassoulides said.
The Greek Cypriot government would be "ready to make concessions provided that this is based on the principle of reciprocity," Cassoulides told a news conference.
Greek and Turkish Cypriot leaders are expected to meet on July 9 in New York under U.N. auspices for their first direct talks in three years about the future of Cyprus, divided since 1974.

Cassoulides later met U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, two days after the White House appointed Richard Holbrooke, who negotiated the 1995 Bosnia peace accord, as special emissary for Cyprus.

The minister hailed the appointment as showing that Washington "means business" in the search for a Cyprus settlement. Greek Cypriots hope the United States will put pressure on Turkey to be more flexible.
In a joint appearance before reporters, Albright assured Cassoulides "of America's interest in seeing the people of Cyprus achieve a lasting settlement to the inter-communal dispute on their island."
She said there could be "no more dramatic a demonstration of that commitment" than President Bill Clinton's decision to assign Holbrooke to the issue.
"We believe that the division of the island is unacceptable," Albright added.
Cassoulides regretted that the New York talks had not been "better prepared" and expressed concern that they should not end in failure, as previous talks have repeatedly done.

"If negotiations were to collapse, this will increase the people's frustration since they have built expectations for a positive outcome." he said. "Similarly, it will erode the faith in the negotiating process and give an opportunity to hardliners from both sides to gain an advantage."
Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash, who will meet Cyprus President Glafcos Clerides in New York, had remained inflexible during recent indirect preparatory talks, he charged.

Mainland Turkish troops invaded Cyprus in 1974 following a short-lived Greek Cypriot military coup in Nicosia. Some 30,000 troops remain in a Turkish-Cypriot mini-state that only Ankara recognises in the northern part of the island.

The expected start of negotiations in the second half of next year to admit Cyprus to the European Union has raised hopes that the two sides may finally be able to agree on the bi-zonal bi-communal federation that both say they want.

Cassoulides said the other development which made next month's negotiations different from previous rounds was the new U.S. interest in the problem, which Albright has marked out as one of her key concerns.
Holbrooke has said he does not plan to take part in next month's talks, but Cassoulides noted that the U.S. envoy lived in New York and was likely to be "around."
